uncertainty_flags: Text-classification probe is a simple summed-vector logistic regression; stronger architectures or fine-tuning could change which pretraining is optimal.
Differences across datasets vary and are sometimes small; one dataset (CR) is an exception.
Only five classification datasets and one corpus; topicality-generalization across domains remains untested.

identified_claims.claim_text: Bound representations tend to benefit sequence-labeling downstream tasks (POS, chunking, NER) because they encode syntactic information.
identified_claims.section_anchor: 3.4 POS, Chunking and NER Tasks; Figure 4; Supplemental Table 7
evidence: Figure 4: Across GSG/GBOW/GloVe and dimensions, dotted (bound) lines are above solid (unbound) lines for POS, chunking, NER.
Table (supplemental) reported POS/Chunking/NER numbers showing consistent bound > unbound e.g., GSG linear word POS 95.3 vs bound 96.0.
uncertainty_flags: Evaluation uses a simple linear classifier over concatenated window embeddings; more powerful sequence models (CRF, BiLSTM-CRF) or fine-tuning might alter relative utility.
Dependency-based contexts show some mixed NER results (dep word vs dep bound), so universality across sequence-labeling tasks is not absolute.
Preprocessing and pruning (freq >=100) could remove infrequent but informative syntactic contexts.

identified_claims.claim_text: Different embedding algorithms (GSG/Skip-Gram, GBOW/CBOW, GloVe) show similar overall tendencies regarding contexts and representations, but GloVe is more sensitive to the choice of context representation.
identified_claims.section_anchor: 3.3 Word Analogy; 3.4 Sequence labeling; Figures and comments
evidence: Text claims and Figures 2-4 show GloVe curves varying more across representation choices; 3.3 explicitly notes GloVe more sensitive and links to its explicit objective.
Observed larger performance swings for GloVe in analogy and sequence-labeling plots.
uncertainty_flags: Qualitative observation; no formal sensitivity analysis (e.g., variance decomposition) provided.
Training regimens differ across algorithms (GloVe 30 iterations vs GSG 2 vs GBOW 5); differences may reflect optimization effort or hyperparameter settings rather than intrinsic sensitivity.
Implementation details in word2vecPM and weighting choices for GloVe may influence observed sensitivity.

identified_claims.claim_text: The authors implemented and will publish word2vecPM, an extension of word2vecf that supports generalized Skip-Gram, CBOW, and GloVe with arbitrary context collections (P, M, M¯).
evidence: 3.1: explicit statement: "We implement word2vecPM toolkit, a further extension of word2vecf... supports generalized SG, CBOW and GloVe with the input of collection P, M and M respectively."
Conclusion: "the word2vecPM toolkit in Supplemental Material will be published online."
uncertainty_flags: Availability, documentation, and exact API/hyperparameter configurations are in supplemental material and contingent on release.
Reproducibility depends on making the exact preprocessing scripts, parse settings, and training configs available; not fully verifiable from main text alone.

identified_claims.claim_text: Pre-trained word embeddings substantially outperform random embeddings on text classification tasks using a simple Neural Bag-of-Words classifier.
evidence: Table 4: Random baseline row shows much lower accuracies (e.g., Random 63.9 vs GSG linear word 76.1 on MR).
Text explicitly: "pre-trained word embeddings outperform random word embeddings by a large margin."
uncertainty_flags: Random baseline details (initialization distribution, dimensionality) not fully described in main text; magnitude of gap could be affected by baseline specifics.
Stronger classifiers or fine-tuning may reduce relative gains from pretraining, though the empirical result aligns with standard literature.

strengths.title: Comprehensive factorial empirical design
strengths.description: The paper systematically crosses context type (linear vs dependency) × representation (bound vs unbound) × algorithm (GSG, GBOW, GloVe) and reports results across many intrinsic and extrinsic tasks and embedding dimensionalities.
evidence: Manuscript: full experimental matrix across Figures 2-4 and Tables 4-7; training details in 3.1; supplementary numeric tables.

strengths.title: Reproducibility-oriented artifact (word2vecPM)
strengths.description: Authors extend existing toolkits and promise a released implementation supporting arbitrary context collections, enabling future replication and extensions.
evidence: 3.1: "We implement word2vecPM..." and Conclusion: toolkit will be published; references to word2vecf and code URLs in footnotes.

strengths.title: Task-diverse evaluation with direct probing
strengths.description: Evaluation includes both intrinsic tasks (similarity/analogy) and extrinsic tasks (sequence labeling, classification) using simple, consistent probes to highlight embedding properties.
evidence: Sections 3.2—3.5 describe choice of WordSim, Google analogies, POS/Chunking/NER benchmarks, and five classification datasets; use of linear concatenation probe and summed-vector logistic regression.

concerns.title: No formal effect-size or statistical testing for central comparative claim
concerns.description: The main claim that representation choice has larger impact than context type (C1) is argued via visual inspection of curves and selected numeric tables but lacks statistical quantification (e.g., variance decomposition, ANOVA, bootstrap CIs, or significance testing). Without this, the relative importance statement risks overgeneralization.
evidence: Shared Analysis and manuscript: statements in 2.2, 3.3, and Conclusion rely on observed curve differences; PR reviewers note absence of effect-size tests.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute and report quantitative effect sizes: e.g., run a mixed-effects model or ANOVA with factors representation, context type, algorithm, task and dimension; provide bootstrap confidence intervals and pairwise significance tests for key comparisons (representation vs type) on each task.

concerns.title: Single-corpus and preprocessing/pruning confounds
concerns.description: All experiments use English Wikipedia (Aug 2013) with heavy pruning (ignore words/contexts appearing <100) and lowercasing. Bound/dependency representations increase context vocabulary (authors note ~5x), so pruning and the single corpus could materially bias coverage and performance comparisons.
evidence: 3.1: training details describing Wikipedia, CoreNLP parsing, lowercasing, and pruning threshold <100; 2.2 notes bound representation enlarges context vocabulary ~5x.
Shared analysis flags PRUNE confound and calls for ablations.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run ablations varying pruning thresholds (e.g., >=5, >=50, >=100) and report resulting vocabulary sizes and re-run key comparisons; add at least one other corpus (e.g., newswire or web crawl subset) to test generality.

concerns.title: Dependency parsing and collapsing choices not ablated
concerns.description: Dependency-based contexts depend on parser quality and preprocessing choices (collapsed prepositions). The paper does not test sensitivity to parser errors, parser choice, or collapsing vs not collapsing prepositions, which could influence dependency-context effectiveness.
evidence: 2.1 and Figure 1: authors collapse prepositions and use Stanford CoreNLP; Shared Analysis notes parser and collapsing are implicit assumptions (A1, A2).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report parser accuracy or sample parsing quality; ablate collapsing prepositions (run experiments with and without collapsing) and, if feasible, test a second parser (e.g., UDPipe or spaCy) on a subset to gauge sensitivity.

concerns.title: Unequal training parity and hyperparameter confounds across algorithms
concerns.description: Different iteration counts and negative sampling settings were used across algorithms (GSG: 2 iterations, GBOW: 5, GloVe: 30), and GBOW negative sampling differs from GSG. These differences may explain apparent algorithmic sensitivity (GloVe) or mixed GBOW behavior rather than intrinsic algorithm properties.
evidence: 3.1 Training Details: iteration counts and negative sampling sizes listed; Shared Analysis flagged training parity concern (A6).
3.3 and 3.4 attribute greater sensitivity to GloVe without systematic parity control.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run controlled training-parity experiments: fix iterations and comparable optimization effort across models or report learning curves per iteration; sweep negative-sampling and learning rate to show conclusions robust to these settings.

concerns.title: Downstream probe simplicity limits external validity
concerns.description: Sequence-labeling uses a linear classifier on concatenated window embeddings and text-classification uses summed embeddings + logistic regression. These simple probes expose embedding properties but may not reflect performance when embeddings are used with more powerful/fine-tunable models (BiLSTM-CRF, CNNs, Transformers).
evidence: 3.4 and 3.5 describe intentionally simple probes; Shared Analysis and prior reviewers recommend testing stronger downstream models.
Prior literature (Schnabel et al., 2015; Linzen, 2016; Chiu et al., 2016) noted intrinsic metrics don't reliably predict extrinsic performance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add at least one stronger downstream model per task family (e.g., CRF or BiLSTM-CRF for sequence labeling; CNN/LSTM or fine-tuned classifier for text classification) on a subset of settings to demonstrate whether observed preferences persist.

concerns.title: Limited external benchmarks for functional/topical claims
concerns.description: Functional vs topical conclusions are mostly supported by WordSim353 splits and five classification sets. Broader claims about functional vs topical capture would be stronger with additional benchmarks (e.g., SimLex-999 for genuine similarity, MEN, BLESS, or downstream semantic tasks).
evidence: 3.2 uses WordSim353 similarity/relatedness only; Related Work cites Melamud et al. (2016) and Vulic & Korhonen (2016) that explore related contexts on other datasets/languages.
Shared Analysis recommended other datasets/benchmarks.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add one or two more intrinsic similarity benchmarks (e.g., SimLex-999 for similarity, MEN) and/or a semantic downstream task to triangulate the functional/topical distinction.

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational work on dependency-based contexts, position-aware contexts, and theoretical connections between skip-gram and matrix factorization; manuscript builds on and extends these ideas.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar in examining dependency contexts and bound representations; this paper generalizes to multiple algorithms (GBOW/GloVe) and runs a wider empirical sweep.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior empirical work on context types and dimensionality preferences; raises that intrinsic preferences vary by task.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Melamud et al. compare context types; current paper adds representation axis (bound/unbound) and multiple algorithms, plus toolkit.

comparable_works.relevance: Cross-lingual evidence that dependency-based contexts capture functional similarity in English but may vary across languages.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Supports caution about generalizing single-corpus/English results; the current paper does not test multiple languages.

comparable_works.relevance: Dependency-based embeddings beneficial for parsing; corroborates that dependency contexts encode syntactic signals useful for sequence-oriented tasks.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Aligns with manuscript's POS/sequence-labeling findings but focuses on parsing; current work broader across tasks.

comparable_works.citation_label: Schnabel et al. (2015); Linzen (2016); Chiu et al. (2016)
comparable_works.relevance: Highlight weak correlation between intrinsic evaluations and extrinsic tasks; relevant to interpreting the paper's intrinsic→extrinsic transfer statements.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provide cautionary context suggesting the manuscript's multiple downstream probes are necessary but their simple probes may not cover modern model interactions.

uncertainty_flags: Primary comparative claim (representation > type) is qualitative without formal statistical support; effect magnitudes uncertain.
Single-corpus (Wikipedia) and heavy pruning (freq <100) may bias results, especially for sparse bound/dependency contexts.
Dependency extraction choices (parser, collapsed prepositions) are not ablated; parsing errors could bias dependency-context performance.
Training parity across algorithms differs (iterations, negative-sampling), confounding algorithm-sensitivity claims (notably GloVe).
Downstream probes are intentionally simple linear models; interaction with stronger models or fine-tuning is unknown.
alternative_interpretations: Observed advantages of bound representations for sequence labeling could partly reflect differential vocabulary coverage due to pruning: bound contexts produce many rare context types which may be pruned differently than linear contexts, leaving a filtered subset that incidentally favors syntactic distinctions.

GloVe's greater variability across representation choices might be due to differing training iterations and objective weighting dynamics rather than intrinsic sensitivity; with matched optimization effort differences could shrink.

GBOW's inconsistent patterns (e.g., dependency-unbound performing poorly on similarity) could stem from the authors' role-exchange in GBOW (predicting words from summed contexts) and its interaction with sparse dependency contexts, rather than a fundamental mismatch between GBOW and dependency contexts.
transparency_notes: Exact code, preprocessing scripts, CoreNLP version and parser settings, full config files for word2vecPM, and the supplemental numeric tables should be published with the toolkit to enable replication.
Reporting vocabulary sizes (words and contexts) after pruning for each context × representation variant and per-dimension would clarify coverage differences and help diagnose pruning confounds.
Presenting per-run random seeds or multiple random restarts for stochastic trainings (and reporting variability) would increase confidence in the reported curves.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Although prior work has compared context types (e.g., Levy & Goldberg, Melamud et al.), explicit, systematic crossing of context type × representation × algorithm with a toolkit implementing GBOW and GloVe on arbitrary contexts appears to be a relatively new and useful empirical contribution. Novelty here is an incremental empirical/systematization advance rather than a theoretical breakthrough; novelty does not substitute for robustness checks.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If pruning thresholds are lowered (increasing coverage) and results persist, the representation > type claim becomes stronger.
If alternative corpora (newswire, web crawl) and at least one other parser yield similar patterns, generalizability would be supported.
If statistical effect-size analysis demonstrates representation explains more variance than type across tasks and models, the main claim would be quantitatively validated.
If matched training parity across algorithms leaves GloVe more variable, then algorithmic sensitivity is likely intrinsic rather than an optimization artifact.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The work systematizes two orthogonal context axes (type and representation) across multiple embedding algorithms and tasks, and supplies an implementation (word2vecPM). This fills a methodological gap by enabling consistent comparisons beyond earlier single-algorithm or single-axis studies.
evidence: Comprehensive experiments across GSG/GBOW/GloVe and tasks; explicit toolkit implementation in 3.1 and supplemental material.
uncertainty_flags: Degree of systematization is high, but the impact depends on addressing robustness/ablation concerns (pruning, corpus, parser, training parity).

novelty_lenses.rationale: Because the work interprets representation effects as generally larger than type effects, this interpretive novelty is potentially impactful, but its generality is not yet firmly established — risk arises if operational choices cause the effect.
evidence: Authors' core claim (C1) contrasted with potential confounds identified (pruning, single corpus, hyperparameter differences).
uncertainty_flags: Empirical novelty is present but could be fragile to ablations.

confidence_interval.rationale: My confidence that the reported directional effects (e.g., bound aiding sequence-labeling; linear-unbound better for topical relatedness and classification) are real in the reported experimental setup is high (supported by multiple plots and numeric tables). However, my confidence that the central general claim (representation choice > context type in importance) generalizes broadly across corpora, preprocessing thresholds, parser choices, training parity, and stronger downstream models is moderate to low without additional robustness analyses. The interval reflects strong confidence in within-experiment observations but more uncertainty about external generalization and effect-size quantification.

consensus_findings: The manuscript presents a broad, systematic empirical comparison crossing context type (linear vs dependency) and context representation (bound vs unbound) across three embedding algorithms (generalized Skip-Gram, generalized CBOW, and GloVe) and multiple intrinsic and extrinsic tasks.

Within the reported experimental setup (English Wikipedia, specified preprocessing and hyperparameters, simple downstream probes), consistent directional patterns are observed: bound representations tend to emphasize syntactic/functional signals and improve sequence-labeling and functional-similarity probes, while unbound linear contexts tend to preserve topical co-occurrence signals and perform better on relatedness and simple text-classification probes.

The authors implemented an extended toolkit (word2vecPM) that generalizes prior tooling (word2vecf) to permit arbitrary context collections for SG/CBOW/GloVe; the toolkit is intended for release and supports the controlled experiments reported.

GloVe appears to show larger qualitative sensitivity to the choice of context representation in the reported experiments compared to generalized Skip-Gram and CBOW, though this observation is based on plotted variance rather than formal sensitivity analysis.
disagreements: Degree vs. generality of the central claim that 'representation > type' (C1): reviewers agree the claim is supported descriptively within the paper's experimental regime, but disagree on how strongly to generalize that claim beyond the reported setup. Some reviewers view it as a plausible, broadly useful reframing (if validated), while others caution it is currently a descriptive observation lacking formal effect-size quantification and cross-corpus validation.

Interpretation of GloVe's greater 'sensitivity': reviewers concur that GloVe shows larger score variation across representation choices in the plots, but disagree whether this reflects an intrinsic sensitivity of GloVe's objective or is an artifact of unequal training/optimization budgets and implementation differences.

Sufficiency of downstream probes: reviewers differ on whether the deliberately-simple downstream classifiers are an appropriate and sufficient probe of embedding utility. Some see the simplicity as a strength (isolates embedding signal), others request at least a small set of stronger-model checks to ensure external validity to common pipelines.

Severity of pruning and preprocessing confounds: all reviewers flag pruning/lowercasing as potentially important, but differ on how likely these choices are to materially overturn the reported patterns without further ablations.
uncertainty_hotspots: Single-corpus scope: all experiments trained on English Wikipedia (August 2013). Generalization to other corpora (newswire, web crawl) or languages is untested.

Pruning/vocabulary coverage: the frequency threshold (contexts/words with count <100 removed) interacts with bound representations that multiply context types; differential pruning may change the effective training signal and partly explain representation-driven differences.

Dependency extraction choices: use of Stanford CoreNLP and 'collapsed' preposition arcs are operational choices that may influence dependency-context quality; parser errors and collapsing heuristics were not ablated.

Training-parity across algorithms: different iteration counts and negative-sampling settings were used (e.g., GloVe trained for many more iterations), creating a confound for algorithm-sensitivity claims.

Lack of formal statistical quantification: the core comparative claim (representation effects exceed type effects) is supported by visual inspection and numeric tables but lacks effect-size decomposition, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests across repeated runs.

Downstream-probe external validity: results are obtained using simple linear probes (concatenation window and NBOW sum+logistic); interaction of embedding variants with stronger models (CRF, BiLSTM-CRF, CNN/LSTM, fine-tuning) is unknown.
model_diversity_effects: Across the three embedding families, qualitative task-dependent tendencies are similar: representation choice produces noticeable shifts in behavior across tasks for all algorithms, suggesting the representation axis is an important experimental factor.

Observed algorithm-specific interactions: GBOW shows some divergent behaviors (e.g., worse similarity performance under certain dependency variants), indicating that algorithmic architecture and prediction direction can interact non-trivially with sparse/contextualized context vocabularies.

GloVe demonstrates larger score variance across representation choices in the reported plots; however, this may be confounded by different optimization/regimen settings. Thus model diversity both supports the robustness of some directional patterns (bound vs unbound) and highlights algorithm-dependent caveats requiring matched-training ablations.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Use the reviewers' synthesis to guide a focused revision rather than a blanket acceptance/rejection. Centralize the editor's role by asking authors to (a) quantify the comparative claim (representation vs type) with statistical effect-size analyses (e.g., ANOVA/mixed-effects, bootstrap CIs, variance decomposition) across key tasks; (b) perform a small but targeted set of robustness checks addressing the largest uncertainty hotspots: replicate representative experiments on at least one additional corpus (e.g., newswire or a web-crawl subset), report post-pruning vocabulary counts per condition and rerun a pruning-threshold ablation (e.g., thresholds 5/50/100), and equalize training effort across algorithms or present sensitivity to iteration budget; (c) add at least one stronger downstream probe per family (e.g., BiLSTM-CRF for sequence labeling and a CNN/LSTM or fine-tuned classifier for text classification) to assess external validity; and (d) release the word2vecPM toolkit with preprocessing scripts, config files, and a README reproducing at least one main figure/table. If authors address these targeted items and the patterns remain, consider the claims empirically well-supported within broader generality bounds.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and reproducibility, provide the following: (1) Quantitative effect-size analyses supporting the representation>type claim: run ANOVA or mixed-effects models, compute percent variance explained by representation vs type across tasks, and include bootstrap confidence intervals or paired significance tests over multiple random seeds. (2) Pruning and coverage diagnostics: report vocabulary and context-type counts after pruning for each context/repr variant; run sensitivity experiments with lower pruning thresholds (e.g., 5, 50, 100) and report whether main patterns persist. (3) Cross-corpus check: rerun a small but representative subset of experiments (e.g., GSG and one dimension setting for WS353 similarity, POS, and one classification dataset) on an additional corpus (newswire or a CommonCrawl subset) and report results. (4) Parser/dep-extraction ablation: for dependency-based contexts, compare collapsed vs non-collapsed prepositions and (if feasible) one alternative parser on a subset to assess robustness. (5) Training-parity control: equalize or justify differing iteration counts/negative-sampling across algorithms, or present learning curves/conv ergence diagnostics to show observed algorithmic sensitivity is not merely an optimization artifact. (6) Downstream robustness: add at least one stronger downstream architecture per task family (e.g., BiLSTM-CRF for sequence-labeling; CNN/LSTM or fine-tuned classifier for text classification) as a sanity check. (7) Release artifacts: publish word2vecPM and provide preprocessing scripts, exact command-lines/configs, random seeds, and a short reproduction guide reproducing a key figure/table.
transparency_report: The manuscript documents many implementation and experimental details (corpus used, parser, preprocessing, pruning threshold, hyperparameters, per-model iteration counts) and provides numeric supplemental tables; this is a strong reproducibility baseline.

However, missing items limit exact replication and interpretation: (a) post-pruning vocabulary/context counts per condition; (b) random seeds or multiple-run variance estimates; (c) exact preprocessing scripts and parser configuration; (d) matching/training-parity rationale between algorithms; and (e) the toolkit (word2vecPM) and supplemental numeric tables are described as forthcoming rather than immediately available.

Providing the above items in a public repository (code, scripts, config files, data extraction steps, seeds, and README with commands to reproduce at least one main result) would substantially increase transparency and enable independent validation.
epistemic_limits: All synthesized conclusions are conditional on the reported experimental regime (English Wikipedia corpus, given preprocessing and pruning, window size and model hyperparameters, and simple downstream probes). The core comparative claim (representation influences > type influences) is currently supported by descriptive empirical patterns within that regime but lacks formal effect-size quantification and cross-corpus/language or parser/pruning robustness checks; therefore the generality of the claim beyond the reported setup is uncertain. Algorithm-specific conclusions (e.g., GloVe sensitivity) are confounded by unequal training/optimization budgets and require controlled parity experiments to attribute causes. Finally, simple downstream probes isolate embedding properties but do not fully characterize interactions with modern, fine-tuned models; observed task-preferences may attenuate or invert when embeddings are used in richer architectures.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This manuscript reports a systematic, factorial empirical study comparing two context types (linear window vs dependency-based) and two context representations (bound vs unbound) across three embedding algorithms (generalized Skip-Gram, generalized CBOW, and GloVe). Trained on English Wikipedia and implemented via an extended toolkit (word2vecPM), the experiments cover intrinsic evaluations (WordSim353 similarity/relatedness splits, Google analogies) and extrinsic tasks (POS, chunking, NER with a linear-window probe; five sentence/document classification datasets with a summed-vector probe). Within the reported setup the authors observe consistent directional patterns: bound representations accentuate syntactic/functional signals (helping functional-similarity probes and sequence-labeling), while unbound linear contexts preserve topical co-occurrence (helping relatedness and simple text-classification). They further note algorithm-dependent interactions (GBOW idiosyncrasies) and qualitatively larger representation-sensitivity for GloVe. The paper contributes an empirical map of these choices and a toolkit enabling arbitrary context collections.
strengths: Comprehensive factorial empirical design crossing context type (linear/dependency) × representation (bound/unbound) × algorithm (GSG/GBOW/GloVe) and sweeping embedding dimensionality, reported across multiple intrinsic and extrinsic tasks.

Implementation and planned release of word2vecPM (an extension of word2vecf) that accepts arbitrary context collections and supports GSG/GBOW/GloVe, facilitating reproducibility and follow-up experiments.

Clear, task-aware practical guidance emergent from the experiments (e.g., bound contexts favor syntactic probes/sequence labeling; linear-unbound favors topical relatedness/classification) that can inform practitioner choices.
limitations: Single-corpus scope: All experiments use English Wikipedia (Aug 2013). Corpus-specific register, topical mix, and parsing quality could influence which context choices appear preferable; cross-corpus and cross-lingual generality is not demonstrated.

Pruning and sparsity confound: The preprocessing step discards words/contexts appearing <100 times while bound/dependency representations multiply context types (~5×). Differential pruning may change effective vocabulary and coverage across variants, plausibly inflating or deflating observed representation effects.

Lack of formal effect-size/statistical analysis: The central claim that representation effects exceed context-type effects is supported by plots and tables but lacks quantitative effect-size decomposition (e.g., ANOVA/mixed-effects, percent variance explained, bootstrap CIs) or repeated-run variability estimates.

Training-parity and optimization confounds across algorithms: differing iteration counts and negative sampling settings (e.g., GloVe trained many more iterations than GSG/GBOW) create ambiguity about whether observed algorithm sensitivity (GloVe) is intrinsic or due to unequal training budgets.
open_questions: Can the authors provide quantitative effect-size analyses comparing the contribution of representation vs context type (e.g., ANOVA or mixed-effects models, percent variance explained) and bootstrap confidence intervals across repeated random seeds?

How do post-pruning vocabulary and context-type counts look for each variant (linear/dependency × bound/unbound)? Please report #word types and #context types after pruning and run a sensitivity ablation with lower pruning thresholds (e.g., >=5 and >=50) to show whether the main patterns persist.

Do the reported tendencies replicate on at least one additional corpus (e.g., a newswire or CommonCrawl subset) or on a morphosyntactically different language? If full replication is infeasible, can the authors run a representative subset (e.g., GSG on WS353 similarity, POS, one classification dataset) on another corpus and report results?

Can the authors equalize or justify training effort across algorithms (match effective number of parameter updates/epochs or show learning curves) to rule out optimization-budget explanations for GloVe’s apparent sensitivity?

Would the authors add at least one stronger downstream architecture per task family (e.g., BiLSTM-CRF for sequence labeling; CNN/LSTM or fine-tuned classifier for text classification) as a robustness check to assess whether the simple-probe rankings persist with modern models?

What is the empirical sensitivity to dependency extraction choices? Please ablate the 'collapsed prepositions' heuristic and, if feasible, compare a second parser (or simulated noise) on a small subset to estimate the parser dependence of dependency-context gains.
consensus_snapshot: Across reviewers, the experimental design breadth and the plan to release word2vecPM are seen as solid contributions that enable controlled comparisons.

Within the reported experimental regime (Wikipedia, given preprocessing and probes) the directional patterns are consistent: bound representations favor syntactic/functional signals and sequence-labeling; linear-unbound favors topical relatedness and simple classification probes.

All reviewers flag important methodological and reporting gaps that limit the generality of strong claims: single-corpus dependence, pruning/vocabulary reporting, lack of statistical effect-size quantification, and unequal training/parity across algorithms.
disagreement_snapshot: Extent of generalization of the central claim (representation > type): some reviewers treat it as a plausible, potentially general reframing pending robustness checks; others view it as a within-experiment descriptive observation that should not be generalized without the requested ablations and statistical tests.

Interpretation of GloVe sensitivity: reviewers agree GloVe shows larger variation across variants in the plots but disagree whether this reflects an intrinsic modeling property or optimization/hyperparameter artifacts given unequal iteration counts.

Adequacy of simple downstream probes: some reviewers accept simple linear/NBOW probes as intentional, controlled probes of embedding properties; others request at least a few stronger-model evaluations to assess external validity for modern pipelines.
uncertainty_snapshot: High uncertainty about how pruning threshold and resultant vocabulary differences drive reported effects (pruning may disproportionately remove many bound/dependency contexts).
Medium uncertainty about cross-corpus and cross-lingual generalizability because all experiments use a single English Wikipedia dump.
Medium uncertainty whether GloVe's larger observed sensitivity is intrinsic versus an artifact of unequal optimization/training budgets.
Uncertainty about whether the simple downstream probe rankings persist when embeddings are used inside stronger, fine-tuned models.
source_trace: Levy, O. & Goldberg, Y. (2014). Dependency-based word embeddings: established prior work on DEPS and collapsed dependencies that the manuscript builds on and follows for collapsing prepositions (manuscript cites and reuses their dependency collapsing heuristic).

Ling, W. et al. (2015). Position-aware / structured-skipgram ideas: prior work motivating bound (position-tagged) representations for linear contexts; manuscript extends representation axis across types and algorithms (manuscript cites Ling et al.).

Melamud, O., Goldberger, J., & Dagan, I. (2016). Context type and dimensionality effects: prior empirical work showing task-dependent context preferences which this paper systematizes further (manuscript references Melamud et al.).

Pennington, J., Socher, R., & Manning, C. (2014). GloVe: cited as the matrix-factorization/objective baseline; manuscript compares GloVe sensitivity across representations and algorithms (manuscript describes GloVe variant and training differences).

Levy, O., Goldberg, Y., & Dagan, I. (2015). word2vecf: toolkit allowing arbitrary contexts for Skip-Gram; manuscript implements word2vecPM as an extension to support GBOW/GloVe on arbitrary context collections and cites word2vecf as basis.
transparency_notes: The manuscript documents training corpus, parser, pruning threshold, hyperparameters, and per-algorithm iteration counts, and supplies many numeric tables in supplemental material. Missing elements that limit exact replication and interpretation include post-pruning vocabulary/context counts per condition, random seeds or multiple-run variance estimates, per-algorithm learning curves or convergence diagnostics, and the immediate public availability of word2vecPM plus preprocessing/training scripts and configs. Providing these artifacts and the requested ablation data will materially improve transparency and reproducibility.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request a focused revision addressing the most consequential uncertainty hotspots rather than a full re-run of the entire sweep. Specifically ask authors to (1) provide quantitative effect-size analyses that compare representation vs context-type contributions (e.g., ANOVA/mixed-effects or variance decomposition) with bootstrap CIs over multiple random seeds for key tasks; (2) report post-pruning vocabulary/context counts per variant and run a pruning-threshold sensitivity ablation (e.g., thresholds 5, 50, 100) for representative cases; (3) equalize or justify training budgets across algorithms (or provide learning curves showing robustness) to clarify GloVe sensitivity; (4) run a small cross-corpus replication (representative subset of experiments on a different corpus) and (5) release word2vecPM plus preprocessing/training scripts, configs, and at least one reproduction README. If the authors supply these targeted analyses and the central patterns hold, the manuscript's empirical contributions become substantially more robust and generalizable.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and reproducibility, (a) compute and report effect-size metrics attributing variance to representation vs type (e.g., factorial ANOVA, mixed-effects models, percent variance explained) and provide bootstrap confidence intervals or paired significance tests over multiple random seeds for the primary comparisons; (b) publish post-pruning vocabulary/context counts for each (type × representation) condition and run sensitivity experiments with lower pruning thresholds (e.g., 5 and 50) to show whether patterns persist; (c) equalize effective training effort across algorithms (matched epochs/parameter updates) or show learning curves/convergence diagnostics to rule out optimization artifacts explaining GloVe’s sensitivity; (d) perform a targeted cross-corpus check on a representative subset (e.g., GSG on WS353 similarity, POS, one classification dataset) using another corpus (newswire or CommonCrawl subset) and report results; (e) ablate dependency extraction choices (collapsed vs non-collapsed prepositions and, if feasible, a second parser) on a small scale to estimate parser-dependence; (f) add at least one stronger downstream model per task family (e.g., BiLSTM-CRF for sequence-labeling; a CNN/LSTM or fine-tuned classifier for text classification) as a robustness sanity check; and (g) publicly release word2vecPM with preprocessing and training scripts, config files, random seeds, and a short README that reproduces one main figure/table.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The manuscript provides a wide-ranging empirical comparison of context type (linear vs dependency) and context representation (bound vs unbound) across three embedding algorithms and multiple intrinsic/extrinsic tasks, implemented via an extended toolkit (word2vecPM). Within the experimental regime (English Wikipedia, stated preprocessing and probes) the authors observe consistent directional patterns: bound contexts emphasize syntactic/functional signals benefiting functional similarity and sequence-labeling, while linear/unbound preserves topical co-occurrence beneficial for relatedness and simple classification.

Strengths:
- Broad, factorial experimental sweep enabling direct comparisons across the context axes and algorithms. 
- Practical tooling (word2vecPM) that generalizes prior toolkits to support arbitrary context collections. 
- Actionable, task-aware guidance emerging from the experiments.

Limitations:
- Experiments are confined to one corpus (English Wikipedia); cross-corpus and cross-lingual generalizability are untested. 
- Preprocessing/pruning (removing words/contexts with freq <100) interacts with bound/context sparsity and may differentially alter effective training signal across variants. 
- No formal effect-size or statistical testing is reported to substantiate the central comparative claim that representation effects exceed context-type effects. 
- Unequal training/optimization budgets across algorithms (notably GloVe vs GSG/GBOW) create ambiguity about algorithmic sensitivity conclusions.

Open Questions:
1) Please report vocabulary/context-type counts after pruning for each (type × representation) condition and re-run a pruning-threshold ablation (e.g., thresholds 5, 50, 100). 
2) Provide quantitative effect-size analyses (ANOVA/mixed-effects, percent variance explained) and bootstrap CIs over multiple seeds to support the representation>type claim. 
3) Can a small cross-corpus replication (representative subset) be run to test generality beyond Wikipedia? 
4) Can training parity be matched or learning curves provided to show GloVe’s sensitivity is not an optimization artifact? 
5) Please ablate dependency extraction choices (collapsed vs non-collapsed prepositions and/or a second parser) on a subset. 
6) Will the authors release word2vecPM plus preprocessing/training scripts, configs, seeds, and at least one README to reproduce a main figure/table?

Transparency:
The authors disclose key experimental settings (corpus, parser, pruning threshold, hyperparameters) and provide supplementary numeric tables. Important missing reproducibility elements include post-pruning vocabulary counts, random-seed variability, per-algorithm learning curves/diagnostics, and immediate public access to the toolkit and scripts. Supplying these will materially improve interpretability and reproducibility.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects substantial agreement that the experimental observations are valid within the reported setup (directional patterns across tasks and representation impact). However, substantial methodological and reporting gaps (single-corpus scope, pruning/vocabulary confound, lack of statistical quantification, and unequal training parity) reduce confidence that the strongest general claim (representation consistently matters more than type across corpora, parsers, and model regimes) will hold without qualification. The interval captures moderate confidence in within-experiment findings and lower confidence about broad generalization.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
